Overall workplace ratings across the 30 departments ranged from 40 to 85 (M = 64.63). The histogram shows ratings concentrated around 65, with a somewhat longer tail toward lower ratings and smaller clusters near 45 to 50 and 80. All three predictors were positively associated with rating, and the relationships appear approximately linear. Complaint handling showed the strongest and tightest relationship (r = .83), followed by learning opportunities (r = .62) and pay increases (r = .59). The predictors were also moderately correlated with each other (r = .60 to .67), which may matter when they are entered together. One department with the highest pay-increase score (about 88) had only a moderate overall rating, making it an unusual observation worth keeping in mind. These patterns are consistent with my expectations because all three predictors showed positive, approximately linear associations with rating, and complaint handling showed the strongest relationship.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
2. Specify competing models

Predictions
I expected all three predictors to be positively associated with overall workplace ratings. Handling of employee complaints seemed the most likely to matter. When employees feel that problems are taken seriously and resolved fairly, they are likely to trust their workplace and rate it more favourably overall. Opportunities to learn should explain additional variation beyond complaint handling, because a workplace that supports growth and skill development reflects a different part of employee experience than how problems are managed. Pay increases may also add to the explanation after accounting for complaints and learning, since people tend to view fair compensation as a sign that their work is valued. However, I expected the pay increase to contribute less than the other two, because pay may overlap with the other predictors. For these reasons, I predicted that adding each predictor in turn would improve model fit, with complaints contributing the most.
We will estimate four nested models:








Model
Formula
Purpose




M0: Null
rating ~ 1
Baseline model


M1: Complaints
rating ~ complaints
Evaluate complaint handling


M2: Complaints + Learning
rating ~ complaints + learning
Additional contribution of learning


M3: Expanded
rating ~ complaints + learning + raises
Additional contribution of pay increases





How the complaints coefficient changes
In M1, the complaints coefficient (0.75) describes the association between complaint handling and overall rating with nothing else controlled: departments scoring one point higher on complaint handling were rated about 0.75 points higher overall, on average. In M2, the coefficient (0.64) is the association after holding learning opportunities constant. It is smaller, because part of the M1 association overlapped with learning. In M3, the coefficient (0.65) is the association holding both learning and pay increases constant. It is nearly unchanged from M2, so adding pay increases did not account for any further part of the complaints association. In all three models, complaint handling remained positively associated with rating.

Interpreting the model comparison
M3 explained the largest proportion of variation in rating (R² = 0.7083), but its advantage over M2 (R² = 0.7080) was negligible. Adding complaints to the null model produced the only large improvement (ΔR² = 0.681, p < .001). Adding learning increased explained variance by only 0.027 (p = 0.135), and adding pay increases increased it by 0.0003 (p = 0.876); neither improvement was statistically significant. Adjusted R² rose from 0.670 in M1 to 0.686 in M2, then fell to 0.675 in M3, suggesting that the pay-increase predictor added complexity without adding explanatory value. RMSE fell from 11.97 for the null model to 6.76 for M1, a substantively meaningful reduction, but changed by less than 0.3 rating points with the addition of learning and by almost nothing with the addition of pay increases. Overall, the results suggest that complaint handling is the key predictor of overall rating, and that learning opportunities and pay increases add little once complaints are accounted for.

Residuals versus fitted values showed no clear curvature, with the smoothed line staying close to zero across the range of fitted values, suggesting that a linear specification is adequate for these data. The normal Q-Q plot showed residuals following the reference line through the middle of the distribution, with the most extreme residuals slightly less extreme than a normal distribution would predict. A Shapiro-Wilk test also did not detect a significant departure from normality (W = .945, p = .123), although with only 30 departments this test has limited power. The scale-location plot suggested that residual spread was somewhat larger at low fitted values and smaller in the middle of the range, but there was no clear funnel pattern, so there was no strong evidence of heteroscedasticity. In the residuals-versus-leverage plot, department 24 had the highest leverage but a small residual, and its Cook’s distance (0.17) was well below the conventional cutoffs of 0.5 and 1, so no single department appears to dominate the fitted model. Variance inflation factors were 1.55 for both predictors, well below the usual threshold of 5, so multicollinearity does not appear to be a concern despite the moderate correlation between complaints and learning. Overall, the main assumptions appear reasonably satisfied. Given the small sample, these checks are best read as screening for serious problems, not as proof that the assumptions hold, and I retain reasonable confidence in the model.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
5. Model selection

Why this model
I selected M2 (complaints and learning). The nested F-tests showed that complaint handling significantly improved on the null model (F = 60.7, p < .001), whereas learning (ΔR² = .027, p = .135) and pay increases (ΔR² = .0003, p = .876) did not produce statistically significant improvements. Even so, M2 had the highest adjusted R² (.686, compared with .670 for M1 and .675 for M3) and a lower RMSE than M1 (6.47 compared with 6.76). I rejected M3 because pay increases added essentially nothing and lowered adjusted R². I preferred M2 to M1 because learning opportunities were a theoretically motivated predictor, the diagnostics showed no serious problems, and the added complexity is small. M1 remains a defensible simpler alternative, because the improvement from learning was not statistically significant.

Interpreting the coefficients
Holding learning opportunities constant, a one-point increase in a department’s complaint-handling score was associated with a 0.64-point higher predicted overall rating, 95% CI [0.40, 0.89], p < .001. The interval is entirely positive, so the data are consistent with a clear positive association.
Holding complaint handling constant, a one-point increase in the learning-opportunity score was associated with a 0.21-point higher predicted overall rating, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.49], p = .128. The direction is positive, but the interval includes zero, so the data are also consistent with no association, and this estimate is much less certain than the one for complaints.
Each variable is a department-level score representing the percentage of favourable employee responses, so a one-point difference corresponds to a one-percentage-point difference in the proportion of favourable responses.

The selected model explained approximately 70.8% of the variation in overall workplace ratings across these departments (R² = 0.708; adjusted R² = 0.686). Its in-sample RMSE was 6.47 rating points, meaning that the fitted ratings typically differ from the observed ratings by about that much. This describes fit to these 30 departments, not accuracy for new departments.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
6. Discussion and limitations
Complaint handling was by far the most important predictor of overall workplace ratings. Alone, it explained about 68% of the variation in ratings and was the only addition that significantly improved model fit. Learning opportunities added a small amount beyond complaints, and the improvement was not statistically significant. Pay increases added essentially nothing once complaints and learning were included. This does not mean that learning and pay are unrelated to ratings. The three predictors are moderately correlated with each other (r = .60 to .67), so much of what learning and pay would explain is already captured by complaint handling.
Several limitations apply. The sample contains only 30 departments, so estimates are imprecise (note the wide confidence interval for learning) and statistical tests have limited power. The observations are department-level summaries, so the results describe departments, not individual employees. The data are observational, so the coefficients describe associations, not causal effects. The choice between M1 and M2 rests on adjusted R² and RMSE, not on a statistically significant improvement, so a reader preferring a simpler model could reasonably choose M1. Finally, the reported performance is in-sample and does not show how well the model would predict ratings for new departments.
